before.quote:
For a $d$-dimensional BVP on $[a,b]$, an integer $N\ge1$, uniform mesh width $h=(b-a)/N$, mesh nodes $t_i=a+ih$, and node vector $Y=(Y_0,\ldots,Y_N)\in(\mathbb R^d)^{N+1}$, let $D_h$ be the open set of node vectors for which every midpoint pair $(t_i+h/2,(Y_i+Y_{i+1})/2)$ lies in the vector-field domain and $(Y_0,Y_N)$ lies in the boundary-map domain. Define $G_h:D_h\to(\mathbb R^d)^{N+1}$ by

$$G_{h,i}(Y)=\frac{Y_{i+1}-Y_i}{h}-f\!\left(t_i+\frac h2,\frac{Y_i+Y_{i+1}}2\right)\quad(0\le i<N),\qquad G_{h,N}(Y)=B(Y_0,Y_N).$$

Use the maximum of the Euclidean block norms for both node and residual vectors. The interior rows are normalized by $h$; consequently an unscaled increment row has size $h$ times its normalized row.

Let $y^*\in C^1([a,b],\mathbb R^d)$ solve a square BVP, with $f$ and $B$ continuously differentiable on open neighborhoods of the trajectory and endpoint pair. Put $A(t)=D_yf(t,y^*(t))$, $B_1=D_1B(y^*(a),y^*(b))$, and $B_2=D_2B(y^*(a),y^*(b))$. Let

$$X=C^1([a,b],\mathbb R^d),\quad \|v\|_X=\|v\|_\infty+\|v'\|_\infty,$$

and

$$Z=C([a,b],\mathbb R^d)\times\mathbb R^d,\quad \|(g,q)\|_Z=\max\{\|g\|_\infty,\|q\|_2\}.$$

The **continuous linearized BVP operator** is the bounded linear map $\mathcal L:X\to Z$ given by

$$\mathcal L v=(v'-A v,\ B_1v(a)+B_2v(b)).$$

It is **boundedly invertible** when it is bijective and its inverse $\mathcal L^{-1}:Z\to X$ has finite operator norm. That norm is the conditioning constant for the linearized BVP used in the local discretization theorem.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

before.claim: Write $A(t)=D_yf(t,y^*(t))$ and let $X(t)$ solve $X'=A(t)X$, $X(a)=I_d$. Since $A$ is continuous and bounded on $[a,b]$, extend it continuously by its endpoint values to an open interval containing $[a,b]$. Local existence follows from [F3], and the maximal solution from [F7] is bounded by Gronwall; if it stopped at or before $b$, boundedness of $X'=AX$ would give a finite endpoint limit from which local existence extends it, a contradiction. Thus $X$ exists on $[a,b]$. Define $Q=B_1+B_2X(b)$. If $Qc=0$, then $v(t)=X(t)c$ satisfies $\mathcal Lv=(0,0)$; [F2] forces $v=0$, and $v(a)=c$ then gives $c=0$. The square matrix $Q$ is therefore invertible.

For each mesh let $C_i^h=D_yf(t_i+h/2,(Y_i^*+Y_{i+1}^*)/2)$. Uniform continuity of $y^*$ and $D_yf$ on a compact neighborhood implies $\max_i\|C_i^h-A(t_i+h/2)\|_{\rm op}\to0$. Also $\sup_{h,i}\|C_i^h\|_{\rm op}<\infty$. Applying the chain rule [F5] to the rows in [F1], the interior equation $J_h z=(r_0,\ldots,r_{N-1},q)$ is $(I-hC_i^h/2)z_{i+1}=(I+hC_i^h/2)z_i+h r_i$. For small $h$, $I-hC_i^h/2$ is invertible by its convergent geometric series; its inverse norm is at most $2$, and the induced transition matrices $M_i^h=(I-hC_i^h/2)^{-1}(I+hC_i^h/2)$ satisfy $\|M_i^h\|\le1+C_0h$ for a constant independent of $i,h$.

Let $M_h=M_{N-1}^h\cdots M_0^h$, the discrete homogeneous transfer from $z_0$ to $z_N$. The exact fundamental matrix $X$ satisfies $X(t_{i+1})-X(t_i)=\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}A(t)X(t)dt$. The integrand is uniformly continuous, so its average over each cell differs from its midpoint value by a quantity tending uniformly to zero as $h\to0$. Since $C_i^h-A(t_i+h/2)\to0$ uniformly and $X$ is uniformly continuous, the samples $X(t_i)$ satisfy the implicit-midpoint recurrence with a normalized defect $\eta_i^h$ for which $\max_i\|\eta_i^h\|\to0$. The transition bound in step 1.2 propagates the increment defects $h\eta_i^h$ with total bound at most $C_1(b-a)\max_i\|\eta_i^h\|$; hence $M_h\to X(b)$.

Put $Q_h=B_1+B_2M_h$. By step 2.1, $Q_h\to Q$. Since $Q$ is invertible, determinant continuity makes $Q_h$ invertible for all sufficiently small $h$, and the adjugate formula gives a uniform bound on $\|Q_h^{-1}\|$. For arbitrary forcing blocks $r_i$, the recurrence in step 1.2 and its transition bound give $z_N=M_hz_0+w_h$ and $\max_i\|z_i\|_2\le C_2(\|z_0\|_2+\max_i\|r_i\|_2)$, with $\|w_h\|_2\le C_2\max_i\|r_i\|_2$. The boundary row $B_1z_0+B_2z_N=q$ becomes $Q_hz_0=q-B_2w_h$, so $z_0$ and then every $z_i$ are bounded by $C_3\max(\max_i\|r_i\|_2,\|q\|_2)$ uniformly in $h$.

For every right-hand side $(r_0,\ldots,r_{N-1},q)$, step 3.1 constructs a unique solution of the square linear system $J_hz=(r_0,\ldots,r_{N-1},q)$ and gives the asserted uniform operator bound. Therefore $J_h$ is onto and one-to-one, hence invertible, with the stated estimate.

hypothesis_checks.Volterra: Extend A continuously to an open time interval as current1.1 already does; for each column use D=J×R^d and F(t,z)=A(t)z, continuous on open D. Restrict existing C1 solution to any cell with distinct endpoints h>0; closed cells are order-convex with at least2points. Apply proposition at cell initial value X(t_i)e_j. The same fact licenses the integral equation feeding the existing Gronwall argument in1.1.
hypothesis_checks.integral_norm: H is continuous and each vector H(t)v is continuous and integrable on compact increasing cells. Apply Euclidean vector integral inequality to unit v and take the operator supremum; this proves the matrix norm bound without treating scalar Taylor/FTC as a vector theorem.
hypothesis_checks.defect_bound: Delta_h→0 is current1.2. Both H=AX and X are continuous on compact[a,b], so their moduli tend0 and S_A,S_X finite. Endpoint average differs from X(m_i) by at most omega_X(h/2); its norm is at most S_X. This gives the exact3term bound and hence normalized eta→0; existing propagation then yields M_h→X(b).
hypothesis_checks.choice: No new choice principle; finite column identities, universal unit-vector estimates and explicit suprema suffice.
